$comment: Shared MIME corpus, executed by BOTH backend/internal/pgpmail (Go) and
Two parsers exist because the server never sees a client-protected
account's plaintext, so the browser must re-implement what the server does.
Only the browser's renders mail today: server-side decryption is retired, so
pgpmail.ParseContent is the reference this corpus holds it to rather than a
second live reading. It was one, and the danger is why the corpus exists:
buildPGPDeliveries encrypts ONE plaintext to every To/CC key in a single
call, so recipients on different custody modes received identical ciphertext
under ONE signature, and a disagreement made that one signature authenticate
Audit run-10 found two such disagreements; run-11 found two more. Add a case
here whenever either parser changes; a divergence must fail a test rather

cases.name: named by Content-Type name= only is not a body candidate
cases.why: run-10 finding 1. Go's part.FileName() reads only Content-Disposition, so this part read as unnamed server-side and named browser-side, and the two picked different bodies.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="F1"

--F1
Content-Type: text/plain; name="decoy.txt"

NAMED-VIA-CONTENT-TYPE
--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

THE-REAL-BODY
--F1--

cases.name: named by Content-Disposition filename= only is not a body candidate
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="F1"

--F1
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="decoy.txt"

NAMED-VIA-DISPOSITION
--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

THE-REAL-BODY
--F1--

cases.name: named by both headers is not a body candidate
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="F1"

--F1
Content-Type: text/plain; name="a.txt"
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="b.txt"

NAMED-BY-BOTH
--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

THE-REAL-BODY
--F1--

cases.name: named by neither header wins as the body
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="F1"

--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

FIRST-UNNAMED-WINS
--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

SECOND-IS-DROPPED
--F1--

cases.name: a boundary token inside a part's own text is not a delimiter
cases.why: run-10 finding 2. RFC 2046 5.1.1 makes the delimiter CRLF-anchored; the browser split on the bare token and truncated the body there.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="F1"

--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

Payment is due --F1 unless cancelled in writing.
--F1--
cases.expectBody: Payment is due --F1 unless cancelled in writing.

cases.name: bare LF line endings parse the same as CRLF
cases.why: Go's reader adopts whichever newline it sees first; the browser must not require CRLF.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="F1"

--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

LF-ONLY-BODY
--F1--

cases.name: a preamble before the first delimiter is discarded
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="F1"

This is a MIME preamble for non-aware clients.
--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

BODY-AFTER-PREAMBLE
--F1--

cases.name: text/html wins as html mode
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/alternative; boundary="F1" --F1 Content-Type: text/html

HTML-BODY

--F1--

cases.name: nested multipart is walked in document order
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="OUT"

--OUT
Content-Type: multipart/alternative; boundary="IN"

--IN
Content-Type: text/plain

NESTED-BODY
--IN--

--OUT--

cases.name: text/rfc822-headers is never the display body
cases.why: The protected-headers legacy-display part repeats Subject/From; rendering it shows the user a header dump.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="F1"

--F1
Content-Type: text/rfc822-headers

Subject: Protected Subject
--F1
Content-Type: text/plain

BODY-NOT-HEADERS
--F1--

cases.name: junk after the boundary is not a delimiter line
cases.why: run-11. RFC 2046 5.1.1 allows only transport padding after the boundary. The browser anchored the delimiter's start but not its end, so --B_X split there while Go's reader read it as ordinary content.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B"

--B
Content-Type: text/plain; name="decoy.txt"

NAMED
--B_X
BROWSER-ONLY
--B
Content-Type: text/plain

THE-REAL-BODY
--B--

cases.name: a duplicate Content-Type resolves to the first, not the last
cases.why: run-11. textproto.MIMEHeader.Get returns the FIRST occurrence; the browser used Map.set and took the last, so a part carrying two Content-Type headers classified differently in each parser.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B"

--B
Content-Type: text/plain; name="decoy.txt"
Content-Type: text/plain

LAST-HEADER-WINS
--B
Content-Type: text/plain

THE-REAL-BODY
--B--

cases.name: RFC 2231 name*= names a part, so it is not a body candidate
cases.why: run-11. mime.ParseMediaType decodes name*=utf-8''decoy.txt into a filename so Go skipped the part; the browser's regex matched only a literal name= and treated it as an unnamed body candidate.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B"

--B
Content-Type: text/plain; name*=utf-8''decoy.txt

NAMED-VIA-RFC2231
--B
Content-Type: text/plain

THE-REAL-BODY
--B--

cases.name: RFC 2231 filename*0/filename*1 continuations name a part
cases.why: run-11. Go reassembles the continuation pair into a filename and skips the part; the browser saw no filename= and used it as the display body.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B"

--B
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*0="de"; filename*1="coy.txt"

NAMED-VIA-CONTINUATION
--B
Content-Type: text/plain

THE-REAL-BODY
--B--

cases.name: a close-delimiter lookalike ends the multipart in both parsers
cases.why: run-11. Go's multipart.Reader errors on "--B--junk" and yields no body at all, while the browser skipped that segment and rendered a later part. Both must now yield nothing: the browser stops at the close delimiter instead of stepping over it.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B"

--B
Content-Type: text/plain; name="d.txt"

NAMED
--B--junk
--B
Content-Type: text/plain

BROWSER-ONLY
--B--

cases.name: an uppercase TEXT/PLAIN part is the display body
cases.why: run-11 finding F-01-8. Go selected body candidates with a case-SENSITIVE strings.HasPrefix on the raw Content-Type, while the browser lowercases the media type first, so this part was an attachment server-side and the body browser-side. RFC 2045 media types are case-insensitive.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B"

--B
Content-Type: TEXT/PLAIN

UPPERCASE-IS-STILL-TEXT
--B--

cases.name: an uppercase TEXT/HTML part is the display body in html mode
cases.why: run-11 finding F-01-8. Same case-sensitivity bug, and it also cost the mode: Go's bodyMode already folds case, but the part never reached it.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B" --B Content-Type: TEXT/HTML; charset=UTF-8

Hi

--B--

cases.name: a text/plainish part is not a body candidate
cases.why: run-11 finding F-01-8. Go matched the raw header with HasPrefix, so a made-up subtype that merely STARTS with text/plain won as the body, while the browser compared the whole media type and skipped it — one signature, two readings.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B"

--B
Content-Type: text/plainish

PREFIX-DECOY
--B
Content-Type: text/plain

THE-REAL-BODY
--B--

cases.name: quoted-printable is decoded in a multipart part
cases.why: run-11 finding F-01-8. Go decoded only base64, so the browser showed the text and the server showed the escapes.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="B"

--B
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable

Caf=C3=A9 =
next
--B--

cases.name: quoted-printable is decoded in a single-part entity
cases.why: run-11 finding F-01-8. The non-multipart branch decoded only base64 too.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable

Caf=C3=A9 wrapped =
here

cases.name: trailing whitespace on a quoted-printable line is transport padding
cases.why: run-11 finding F-01-8. RFC 2045 3 drops whitespace at the end of an encoded line; mime/quotedprintable does, and the browser kept it, so the two decoders disagreed on the decoded bytes.
cases.mime:
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable

padded   
next
